definition: Circumstantial means based on surrounding details that suggest a conclusion without directly proving it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word circumstantial. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know circumstantial should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Nobody saw the cat open the pantry, but the circumstantial evidence - flour pawprints and a toppled tin - convinced the whole family.
A suggestive detail merely hints - one receipt raises an eyebrow; circumstantial evidence goes further, stacking surrounding details until they point one way.
An airtight case outranks a circumstantial one: circumstantial details point toward a conclusion, but an airtight case seals every exit an alternative explanation could slip through.

Indirect evidence points at the conclusion without ever stating it - a muddy boot, a late train, a gap in the log. Circumstantial is the courtroom-flavored version of the same route and adds an expectation of stacking: many surrounding details, each pointing one way, until together they persuade.

Secondhand means relayed from someone else's telling - the witness reports what another person claims to have seen. Circumstantial evidence runs the other way: the witness saw the details personally, and only the conclusion is left to inference. Secondhand doubts the source; circumstantial names the route the proof takes.

The word does not mean weak: stacked carefully, circumstantial details can settle a question.
It names the route the proof takes, not its strength.
Circumstantial tells you how evidence points - indirectly, through surrounding details - not how good it is; stacked high, it convicts.

A case can be circumstantial and strong, dubious and checked, unverified and true.

No document ties the unsigned canvas to Elena Vasquez.
No letter mentions it, no gallery ledger lists it, and no one ever saw her paint it.

The museum's case is circumstantial, and the curators say so openly: the canvas was found in her studio building; its pigments match the batch she ordered in 1921; the brushwork leans left, as hers did.
Any one of these facts alone would prove nothing.
Buildings have many tenants, pigments were shared, and other painters favored the left hand.
But the facts arrive together, and they all point in the same direction.
Each one makes the alternatives a little harder to believe.
The label will say 'attributed to' rather than 'by' — the museum's way of admitting that a stack of details, however tall, is still not a signature.
